title: Lessons from a prioritisation process to identify evidence needs at the Woodland Trust, UK
content:
Practitioners need to identify and communicate their research priorities using robust and transparent processes to target effort and foster collaboration between multiple stakeholders. In turn, academics and researchers can maximise engagement with practitioners early in research projects to enable greater practitioner co-design to increase real-world impact and utility for informing EBC.


Abstract

Despite growing acknowledgement and advocacy for the importance of evidence-based conservation (EBC), there remain several challenges for conservation organisations to achieve this in reality. Misaligned incentives between academic research and conservation practice can limit the relevance, applicability and accessibility of research. A further challenge is the low number of practitioner-led research agendas that are published with which academics can engage and enable academic practitioner co-designed research. 149 employees from the Woodland Trust were consulted in a series of facilitated workshops and surveys to produce a practitioner-led research agenda. First, an online survey and consultation meetings took place to gather research and evidence questions. Second, subject matter experts collated and synthesised these questions. Third, workshops were run to refine and score research questions using the criteria of overall priority, urgency and an identifiable pathway to apply research output in conservation practice. This resulted in a research agenda comprising 173 research questions across 14 topic areas. Key lessons learned during this process were: (1) staff time allocated to the prioritisation process enabled multiple additional benefits such as team building, knowledge sharing and cross-team working; (2) allocate time to increase practitioner knowledge of the scientific process and how to identify research, evidence and training needs; (3) establish clear measures of success to monitor progress against research priorities; (4) include external academic and practitioner peer review during the process. Synthesis and applications. Practitioners need to identify and communicate their research priorities using robust and transparent processes to target effort and foster collaboration between multiple stakeholders. In turn, academics and researchers can maximise engagement with practitioners early in research projects to enable greater practitioner co-design to increase real-world impact and utility for informing EBC.
